questions.question: GAAP exists so that financial statements are:
options: Trustworthy and comparable — every reader knows what the figures mean
As flattering as possible to the owner
Kept secret from outsiders
Prepared without any source documents

questions.question: The six Grade 10 principles are:
options: Debit, credit, journal, ledger, trial balance, statements
Historical cost, prudence, materiality, business entity, going concern, matching
Assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses, profit
Honesty, accuracy, speed, neatness, balance, disclosure

questions.question: Scenario questions on GAAP typically ask you to:
options: Recite all six principles in order
Calculate the value of the land today
Identify which principle a described action applies, and explain why
Rewrite the statements without principles

questions.question: Land bought for R650 000 in 2020, valued today at R1 100 000, is shown in the books at:
options: R650 000 — the verifiable purchase price, per historical cost
R1 100 000 — the agent's estimate
The average of the two figures
Whatever the bank prefers

questions.question: Historical cost prefers the purchase price because it is:
options: Always the lowest figure
Easier to remember
A verifiable fact supported by a source document, not a shifting opinion
Required by the estate agent

questions.question: Prudence requires a business to:
options: Record hoped-for profits early
Anticipate possible losses but never record profits before they are certain
Always choose the higher of two values
Ignore doubtful debts until year end

questions.question: The trap that separates historical cost from prudence is:
options: They are the same principle with two names
Historical cost applies to income; prudence to expenses
Prudence sets the price of assets at purchase
Historical cost keeps assets at original purchase price; prudence chooses the cautious estimate under uncertainty

subtopics.title: Materiality and the Business Entity Rule

questions.question: A R60 calculator is recorded as an expense rather than a depreciating fixed asset because:
options: Calculators never last more than a year
The amount is too small to influence any reader's decision — materiality
Equipment is always an expense
The entity rule forbids small assets

questions.question: A R380 000 delivery vehicle, by the same materiality logic, is:
options: Grouped into Sundry expenses
Left out of the books
A fixed asset, tracked separately — the scale demands visibility
Recorded as drawings

questions.question: The owner pays her home electricity from the business bank account. The entity rule requires:
options: Recording it as Drawings — never as a business expense
Recording it as Electricity expense
Ignoring it entirely
Splitting it equally between shop and house

questions.question: The tell-tale sign of a business entity rule scenario is:
options: An asset rising in value
An amount too small to matter
A cost shifted between periods
Phrases like 'the owner took' or 'for personal use'

subtopics.title: Going Concern, Matching, and the Matching Game

questions.question: The going concern principle assumes that the business:
options: Will continue operating into the foreseeable future
Will close within the year
Belongs to its creditors
Must sell its assets at auction values

questions.question: Insurance of R24 000 is paid on 1 April for twelve months; the financial year ends 30 June. This year's insurance expense is:
options: R24 000 — it was paid this year
R6 000 — three months' worth; R18 000 is prepaid for next year
Nil until next year

questions.question: June's last week of wages is only paid in July. Matching requires:
options: Recording the wages in July, when the cash moved
Splitting the wages between the two years equally
Recording them as June's expense, accrued now
Ignoring the wages entirely

questions.question: The self-check for any GAAP scenario is to ask:
options: How large is the amount involved?
Which journal records the transaction?
Who signed the source document?
What is the accountant refusing to do, or insisting on doing?

questions.question: The grandfather who quotes only what he PAID for the farm represents:
options: Historical cost
Prudence
Matching
Materiality

questions.question: The strict aunt with two purses that never mix represents:
options: Going concern
The business entity rule
Historical cost
Prudence

questions.question: The meticulous cousin who pins every cost to the month it served represents:
options: Materiality
Going concern
Matching
The entity rule

questions.question: The owner wants the van shown at its higher current value 'for the bank loan'. The principle that refuses is:
options: Historical cost — the invoice is fact; the higher value is opinion
Materiality — the van is too small to matter
Matching — the van belongs to next year
Going concern — the van will be sold

questions.question: The unrecorded R950 of groceries taken from the shelves calls which relative?
options: The grandmother — prudence
The cousin — matching
The strict aunt — business entity rule: record it as drawings, always
The uncle — materiality

questions.question: Keeping the emigrated customer's R1 500 debt on the books 'in case' offends:
options: Materiality
Prudence — a hope is not an asset; write it off now
Going concern
Historical cost

subtopics.title: Why the Rules Make the Books Believable

questions.question: The treasure all six principles guard is:
options: Speed of recording
The owner's privacy
Lower taxes
Believability — statements any stranger can trust

questions.question: Historical cost protects believability because:
options: Nobody can inflate assets to impress a bank — the invoice anchors the figure
It always shows the highest value
It hides the age of the assets
It removes assets from the statements

questions.question: 'Generally accepted' matters because:
options: The rules change for each business
When everyone keeps books by the same rules, everyone can believe everyone's books
Acceptance is optional for sole traders
It allows each accountant a personal rulebook
